notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa025a.opp-l: Chapter 1: 'tu erogare pecuniam meam' appears to have lost a verb (cf. Matt. 25:27, 'you ought to have…'); supplied in brackets. 'Apostoli ,orba' read as 'Apostoli verba'. Chapter 3: 'Quod fuimus faciat' ('let him do what we were') is odd and may be corrupt for 'quod fecimus' ('what we did'); translated as printed. 'Liberati liberate' could also mean 'You who were set free, set free [him]'. Chapter 4: 'Potelil… ns aperire' read as 'Poterit… os aperire'; 'thealio', 'amphitheatio' as theatro, amphitheatro; 'ir.un in die inc' as 'iram in die irae'.

Line 6: 'Verbum intransgressibile' is unusual; rendered 'which does not pass beyond [the Father]', but it may mean 'unchangeable' or 'not passing away'. Line 7: 'et seducitis inultos seducere' read as 'et seductus multos seducere'; 'magnus ubi videris' read as 'magnus tibi videris'. Line 5: the words 'ego enim et Pater non duo dies, sed unus' stand inside the quoted saying to Philip but are not in John 14:9; they appear to be the preacher's gloss.

IX: 'Deus et homo' read for scanned 'Deus ei horto'. X: 'mortalitatem' read as 'immortalitatem' (the sense requires it); 'uoluerunt agnoscere' read as 'noluerunt'. XI: Baruch cited under Jeremiah's name, as often in the Fathers; reference corrected to Bar. 3:36–38 from scanned '5b 58'. XII: 'incaseatos' ('curdled', i.e. rich like cheese) follows the Latin Psalter; 'ter negaverat' read for 'tar'. In XII the second 'Utquid suspicamini...' is put in Christ's mouth with no verb in the Latin; '[might say]' supplied. The Peter quotation is Matt. 16:16; the edition gives 17.

13: 'Quis, quousque descendisti?' read as 'Quid, quousque…'. 15: 'quoniam verius non tacuit' is probably corrupt; read as 'veritas non tacuit' ('the truth did not keep silent'). 16: the Sibylline verses are an acrostic (see the next passage); the printed text carries many stray marginal letters, which are omitted; 'sed enti' read as 'sed cunctae', 'Recidet' as 'Decidet'. In 14, the Luke reference given as 'Id. I, 17' is to 1:76 in substance.

Line 17: 'Itorum' read as 'istorum'. Line 18: 'tremam' read as 'mensam' (table); 'ludentem mortalium mentibus' is obscure in this Latin rendering of the Sibylline Greek and is translated literally. Line 19: 'Nox recondita in diem' is odd; translated as 'night was hidden away within the day'. Line 20: 'scIsSU' read as 'sensu'. Line 21: 'exsufflatis' refers to the exorcistic breathing-out rite used in the Arian rebaptism; 'dccnm ut occidat' is garbled and is read as 'decipis ut occidas' (deceive so as to kill).

The text of all three passages is heavily damaged by scanning; readings were restored by sense. In 22, 'nempiun' is read as 'quempiam' (someone), and the final sentence ('ita venietur et illa') is uncertain. In 23, 'nee tu tuscus' is read as 'nec tu pereas' (that you neither perish); 'rturbitio' is read as 'perturbatio'; 'mUn' is read as 'metu' (fear). In 24, 'spelunca subdola' (deceitful cave) is as printed, but it may be corrupt. The Jeremiah quotation follows the text's own wording.

nodes.text: SERMON ON THE CREED AGAINST JEWS, PAGANS AND ARIANS.

CHAPTER ONE. Christian vigils. Amid the pressures and distresses of the present time, and the duties of our service, we are compelled, dearly beloved, not to keep silent, though it would rather be fitting to weep than to say anything. Nevertheless, so that, bringing too little profit to the Lord's treasury, we may not be told, 'Wicked and lazy servant, you [ought to have] paid out my money, and I on coming would have demanded it back with interest' (Matt. 25:26–27), I ask your Charity to be pleased to receive gladly what the master of the house himself will have served to you through us. These are the Apostle's words: 'The night is far gone, and the day has drawn near; so, putting off the works of darkness, put on the armour of light' (Rom. 13:12). And so, with the gloom of night driven out and the darkness of sins put to flight, let the ray of the true light shine in our hearts. For the purpose of this great assembly requires of us both to give you an account of the night just past, and to show the true and everlasting salvation of this day, from so great a sacrament received. For if we consider the works of the past night, and are able, by the Lord's gift, to set out what we have done, we shall find that in the night we have performed not the works of night but those of day. For we did not find our senses lulled by the pleasure of sleep, nor our souls deluded by phantoms, nor did rest bend down our bodies, weighed down by the warmth of bedding, into deep slumber: but by keeping vigil, praying, singing psalms, fighting against the adversary, the devil, we both felt a great light poured into our hearts and performed in the night the works of day. For what did we do this night? We put the devil to flight, we brought Christ in. What did we do this night? We took captive the captor. What did we do this night? We shut out the devil's darkness from your hearts; we showed that the true light must be drunk in. What was done this night? True strength came and bound the strong man, and plundered the vessels of his house (Matt. 12). What was done this night? Pride was rooted out, humility was brought in. What was done this night? The prince of all vices was driven out, the fount of all good things was received. You see, dearly beloved, what good things you have prepared for you, and from what load, or from what burdens of sins, you are relieved by him who calls you to take up his gentle yoke and his light burden (Matt. 11:29–30). 'So, putting off the works of darkness, put on the armour of light.' Know that what this means has been set out to you from the words of the Creed which you have just received. What is 'Put off the works of darkness' but 'Renounce the devil, his pomps and his angels'? And what is 'Put on the armour of light' but 'Believe in God the Father almighty'?

CHAPTER II. Who the devil is. First, however, dearly beloved, let us examine who or what the devil is, and what his pomps are, by renouncing which we put off the works of darkness; then at last we shall speak to your Charity about God the Father almighty, who is the true light, as far as he himself grants. What is the devil? An angel separated from God through pride, who did not stand in the truth, the author of lying, and deceived by himself, who desired to deceive another. He became the adversary of the human race, the inventor of death, the founder of pride, the root of malice, the head of crimes, the prince of all vices, and the persuader to shameful pleasures too. When he looked on that first man, namely Adam, the father of us all, and saw man made from the mud of the earth in the image of God, adorned with chastity, ordered by temperance, surrounded by charity, clothed with immortality, he, jealous and envious that an earthly man had received these things, which he himself, while he was an angel, is known to have lost through pride, at once, insatiable murderer, envied him, and stripped those our first parents of those gifts and such great goods, and killed them besides. For, dearly beloved, when the devil had taken from man such great goods, chastity, continence, charity, immortality, and had rendered him naked and shameful, he mocked him, covered in his own rags, bound him to his dominion, and by that bond made all his offspring liable to himself. For Adam received shameful rags when, stripped of chastity by the devil, he was girded with unchastity; having lost temperance, he became intemperate; having lost charity, he was found evil; stripped of immortality, he was handed over to death. Alas! What he lost, and what he received! To these most shameful rags he also bound his descendants.

CHAPTER III. What it is to renounce Satan. Let us renounce this ruinous inheritance: we have been made orphans. Before the collector comes, if anyone neglects to renounce so evil an inheritance, in which are the devil's rags, namely his pomps and his angels, when the judge comes, as the Gospel says, the debtor will be handed over to the collector, and the collector will thrust the debtor into prison. 'Amen I say to you,' says the Lord, 'you will not come out from there until you pay the last farthing' (Matt. 5:26). And so divine Scripture commends the whole human race as a poor man and an orphan, saying to God, 'To you the poor man is left; you will be the orphan's helper.' And pointing out his adversary, the devil, it went on to add, 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man' (Ps. 9:35–36 [10:14–15 Heb.]). So let some devout person be present and show some mercy to this orphan and poor man. For he suffers a fierce and cunning adversary, and this orphan fails in his case, since his adversary has bound him by wicked deeds. Let us provide this orphan with fit defenders, and let us put in place for him the advocacy of the Apostles as heavenly jurists. What must be done before such men for such a one? Before you, then, Peter, Paul, John, and the other holy counsellors of the true judge, friends of the highest power, we set out the case, which you know very well, of this poor man and orphan, namely the human race, who, found a debtor and guilty by his father's bond, is held fast and bound by the adversary: there is no other way for him to be helped except by your counsel. So whatever seems good to your serenity in this matter for the freedom of this wretch, be pleased, after common deliberation, to deliver a united judgement on his behalf. For this obligation had bound you too, had grace not come to your aid. Set free, set free: bring out the counsel you received from the true judge, so that he who is held captive may follow it and, through your defence, pass from evil servitude to true freedom. And this is the voice of all: 'Let him do what we were.' What, I ask, is he to do? Let him renounce the devil, his pomps and his angels: this is that ruinous inheritance which we are compelled to renounce. You see, dearly beloved, what judgement our defenders have delivered.

CHAPTER IV. Relapse after Baptism. So let each one keep watch, lest, not renouncing wholly after his profession, the devil recognise his own rags on him, and he begin to be held guilty for ever whom Christ wished to free by his grace. Nor let those flatter themselves who after receiving grace refuse to be corrected and go back again to those former pleasures of theirs. For the day of judgement is awaited; that most just judge will be present, who will respect the person of no powerful man, whose palace no one will corrupt with gold or silver. All souls will stand there, that each may receive according to what it did through the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). For the adversary, the devil, will also be at hand; the words of our profession will be read out. And if anyone is found such that he departs this life a debtor, that adversary will exult in the sight of the most severe judge, crying that he has the upper hand, pleading such a case before such a judge: 'Most just judge,' he says, 'judge justly: justice and judgement are the preparation of your throne (Ps. 88:15). Judge him to be mine who refused to be yours: he is mine, he must be condemned with me. After his renunciation, why did he seize my rags? What was unchastity doing with him, which he had renounced? What was intemperance, what avarice, what anger, what pride, what the rest of my things [doing]? Lastly, most just one: fleeing from me, taking refuge with you, he was afterwards caught by me with my things, which he had renounced; I held him as a trespasser: he was caught by me, as it were, on my own property. For what was he doing in the circus, sharing out to himself there frenzies, quarrels, mad shouts and empty victories, when he had already made them foreign to himself? What was the renouncer of shameful pleasures doing in the theatre? What [was he doing] in the amphitheatre, gazing on cruelties with his own eyes? He stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5). All these things of mine he seized after his renunciation; he wished to be mine, and he coveted my things. Judge, most just judge, since he whom you deigned to free at so great a price afterwards wished to bind himself to me.' Will he, dearly beloved, be able to open his mouth, who after his profession is found such that he is justly handed over to the devil? See what you are doing, my sons, my brothers; see what you are doing, how you keep this profession of yours. We adjure you by the judge himself and all the heavenly powers, which both hear us admonishing and receive you professing, that you do not receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor. 6:1), but with an undivided heart, with all your strength, with perfect faith renounce and spurn so ruinous a diabolical inheritance, so that you may not remain orphans or poor.

CHAPTER V. — The unity of the Trinity. Believe in God the Father almighty. Changing your Father, change your inheritance. Who is this Father almighty? We who believe know that God is indeed our Father, and the Father of the whole world, by grace; but we also seek his own Son by substance, since even before the world was formed by him, he was Father. If he was Father, whose Father was he? He certainly had a Son, from himself and with himself, the same as he is, but not himself; for that one is the Father, this one the Son. For the almighty Father begot from himself an almighty Son, so equal to himself that he remained wholly in himself, and was Father of the Son, and the Son [was Son] of the Father, God from God, day from day, light from light: and yet not two gods, or two days, or two lights, but one God, one day, one light. You do not grasp it by seeing; understand it by believing. Cleanse the eyes of the heart; or rather, let the very light you desire to see cleanse your heart, so that it may be cleansed of the darkness of sins: for Blessed are the clean of heart, because they shall see God (Matt. 5:8). Look, stretch out the sight of the eye of the heart and see; turn the ear of the heart and hear. For 'Father' and 'Son' sound like two; but when the Son himself says, I am in the Father, and the Father is in me (John 14:10), [we see that] the Son is the Word of the Father; and the Father was never without the Word, since In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: this was in the beginning with God (ibid. 1:1). Since this Word, the Son, is in the Father, and the Father in his Son, his Word, they are therefore not two gods, but there is one God. 'Day from day' seems to signify two days: but the Son himself in the Gospel says to the Jews, Abraham your father longed to see my day, and he saw it, and rejoiced (ibid. 8:56); and Abraham, seeing three men under the oak of Mamre, did not call them three lords, but in all of them called upon one Lord, as three [persons] one day. Hence the Lord himself in the Gospel, wishing the Father and the Son to be understood as one day, [answered] Philip, who was asking for the Father as if for another day, since he already saw the Son as day, showing him with what eye he ought to seek to see the unity of God, because he had fixed the eye of the flesh on the humanity: Philip, he said, whoever has seen me has seen the Father too; for I and the Father are not two days, but one. If you can grasp it, grasp the everlasting day.

CHAPTER VI. — The Trinity is incomprehensible. 'Light from light' seems to sound like two lights: but far be it from us that the error of the Manichaeans should take hold of us, who think that this sun is Christ. We, rather, believe that the sun of justice is the Word of the Father, inseparable, equal, abiding with the Father, and ordering all things with him: the Father making all things through the Son, building the fabric of the world through his Word; the Son coming to us, and not deserting the Father, always with him, nowhere without him; giving light, and shining, beaming, flashing both from himself and from him: not two lights, but one light. For I, he says, and the Father are one (ibid. 10:30). Of this only-begotten Word the prophet David says: Once God has spoken, these two things I have heard (Ps. 61:12). How did God speak once, and sound a second time, unless because the Word, which does not pass beyond [the Father], proceeding from the heart of the Father, took on flesh from the womb of a mother, so as to be man? He came, and he remained: he came to us, and did not withdraw from the Father. See, through God's speaking once, our whole fabric arose; through his sounding a second time, he became our peace, so as to dissolve enmities in the flesh (Eph. 2:14). Not regarding this Word, this light, the Arian dares to call the Son lesser, whom we confess equal: with insane obstinacy he wishes to dispute about the Word abiding in the heart of the Father, when he cannot understand himself. Insane heretic, first return to yourself, consider the whole of yourself, if you can comprehend yourself: and then dispute about him who made both me and you. See how that humble man did not think high things, but sought to know God in simplicity of heart, he who with one stone brought down the proud brow of Goliath (1 Sam. 17:49). See how he did not think high things: for he considered what went on in himself; he considered his soul, looked into his own fabric, examined within himself what he was, and from what part he governed so beautiful a bulk, and how in an earthen vessel the soul dwelt as mistress, full of such treasures of wisdom, knowledge and prudence; where such great, such precious, such grand things were there; what places the soul occupied, in which there is no place; and how from one spring the individual powers proceeded without diminishing either what goes out or what pours forth. He saw these things, he considered these things, he wished but was not able to comprehend them, and cried out to God, saying: Your knowledge has been made wonderful beyond me; it has grown strong, and I shall not be able [to reach] it (Ps. 138:6). This was to say: When can I comprehend you, so great, I who cannot unfold myself, the least and small? See also another humble man, seeking out the measure of his own weakness, and not going beyond it, but bending down to lowly things: The sand of the sea, he says, and the drops of rain, and the days of the age, who has numbered? The height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss, who has measured? The wisdom of God that goes before all things, who has searched out (Ecclus. 1:2–3)? See, the prophet says, or rather the Lord himself who spoke through the prophet, that no one has searched out the wisdom of God. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). No one has been able to search out the wisdom of God according to the divinity: because, in respect of the Son being born of the Father without a mother, who shall declare his generation (Isa. 53:8)?

CHAPTER VII. — Against the Arians. Tell me, heretic, you who dare to say that the Wisdom of God is lesser: tell me, how great is the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, the depth of the abyss? Count, if you can, the drops of rain, the sand of the sea, and the days of the age; show me also the number of your hairs, since all the hairs of your head are numbered (Matt. 10:30), and explain these small lower things, and then I will believe that you can search out the higher things. But you cannot, you are not able. The Spirit of God convicts you, who foresaw you heretics beforehand. For those who wrote and perceived the things we have spoken of above were moved by the spirit of truth, not of error. But you, heretic, though you cannot explain these things, dare to dispute about the very Wisdom of God, which cannot be searched out: and you seem great to yourself, because you dispute with no one arguing against you, no judge presiding. And while the times favour your error, you think yourself something, though you are nothing: and, having been led astray, you long to lead many astray, some by money, some by power: you gather such people to yourself, so that you may destroy very many along with you. This labour of yours is not useful for salvation, but rather for ruin. For by teaching such things, or rather not teaching but blaspheming, you are shown to do injury not to some powerful man, but to God the Father himself in his Son. 'The Father is greater, the Son is lesser: the Father is better, the Son inferior.' Not even any wise man would willingly accept these insults, who strives to have a son better than himself, or equal. Hence also that prophetic saying: The father rejoiced in a wise son; in his life he saw [it], and at his death he was not saddened. For the father died, and it is as though he had not died: for he left behind him one like himself (Ecclus. 30:4–5). See, the prophet says that the wise son of a man is like his father; and you, heretic, dare to say that Wisdom itself, that is, the Son of God, is unlike the Father? The prophet says that a man's father, though dead, lives in his son in that he left a son like himself: and you dare to separate eternal Life itself, which is the Son of God, from the Father, who never dies?

CHAPTER VIII. — The equality of the persons. 'And what am I to do?' you say. 'He himself said, The Father is greater than I (John 14:28).' Because you do not understand, what he said well sounds ill to you. For he did say it; indeed he even confirmed it. He certainly said it: The Father is greater than I; the Son himself said it. But see when he said it: he said it when placed in the assumption of human nature. He said, The Father is greater than I, at the time when he said, My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt. 26:38). He said, The Father is greater than I, when he wept, when he was weary, when he hungered, when he thirsted. He said, The Father is greater than I, when Scripture says he was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6). For surely your insane pride does not go so far in irreverence here as to dare to say that the Word of God, abiding with the Father, is in that very divinity lower than the angels? If you do not dare to say this, heretic, keep to these steps, and your error perishes: the Son is equal with the Father and beside the Father, since he is everlasting with the everlasting, always abiding with the always abiding; equal [when] sent and coming; in the assumption of man lesser, not only than the Father, but also than the angels; equal in the form of God, lesser in the form of a servant; equal with the Father in creating angels, lesser than the Father in making men angels; equal with the Father in building a new world, lesser than the Father in restoring a lost world; equal with the Father in bestowing eternal life, lesser than the Father in taking on our death.

CHAPTER IX. — The birth of Christ. This Son of God, then, we believe to be lesser in the assumption of man, equal to the Father in divinity, made, as the Apostle says, of the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3). For the virgin Mary was of the seed of David; she conceived of the Holy Spirit, and in her womb, the Word having taken on flesh, there was made for us a mediator, wholly man and God (1 Tim. 2:5), the Word and soul and flesh one Christ. This indeed the order of this sacrament also declares to us: that after we believe in God the Father almighty, we believe also in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary. And this birth confounds all human thought, since divine power brought it about. For when does the reasoning of our generation admit that a virgin conceiving, a virgin remaining after the birth, should be seen [to have] a Son, and her integrity be kept inviolate? This no man born can accomplish; but he could, because he was not man alone, but God and man; who willed to be born a man for this reason, because every man had perished. So the first great and singular miracle of this Mediator was that he was born thus: so that he who came to teach many to do miracles, which he did both by himself and through them, should yet have something of his own, he who had usurped nothing belonging to another. For he alone was born of a virgin, because he alone was conceived of the Holy Spirit without the embrace of male and female; he alone filled his mother's womb without corruption, because he alone ascended above the heavens for us, to sit at the right hand of the Father. The disciples received from him the power to do many and great miracles, and they did them; yet none of them is preached or believed to have been born of a virgin, or conceived of the Holy Spirit, except that one who, the creator of times, was found in time and was himself also created, taking up the human nature which he had formed whole, so that through it, as redeemer, he might in a certain manner repair our ruin. And he is the Son of God and the son of man: the Son of God in the heart of the Father, the son of man in the womb of his mother; the very same one Christ, who came forth from the virginal womb as a bridegroom from his chamber (Ps. 18:6). In that womb a spiritual marriage was celebrated, and God was joined to flesh, and flesh cleaved to God, so that there should be one Christ, God and man.

CHAPTER X. — The cruelty of Herod. From there, then, he came forth as a bridegroom from his chamber, and at his marriage the whole of creation was seen to be stirred and to exult. For the choir of angels, from this marriage, proclaims peace to men of good will: because he who was the Son of God was made also the Son of man, taking up what he was not, not losing what he was. For this marriage the heavens bring forth a new star, a new and splendid light, that bridegroom himself working in them, so that they might announce the true light to those sitting in the shadow of death, and as with their own tongue praise this bridegroom coming forth, whom they knew to have taken up mortal man in order to make him immortal. To this bridegroom the Magi come from the ends of the earth; forewarned, they seek him; called, they offer gifts, not yet seeing the newborn infant, but with the star as guide desiring to adore the king. At this marriage of the newborn king Herod was troubled, and troubled too were the Jews, not understanding the king of all creation. Herod seeks to destroy the infant whom he hears born king, lest as he grew he might lose his kingdom; the Jews, unwilling to have the Son of God as king, betray to Herod where the Christ was to be born, and the will of both is bound together upon the slaying of one infant. After Herod learned from the Jews' account where the Christ who was to be killed might be found, calling the Magi to him he inquired of them the time of the star, and sending them to Bethlehem he said: Go, inquire diligently about the child, so that I too may come and adore him (Matt. 2:8). O deceitful lips! Why do you speak evil with one heart and another? For your tongue holds one thing, your conscience cries out another. You deceive yourself by thinking such things; you go astray, you deceive and are deceived. In vain does falsehood keep watch in evil: the truth is not sought by you as it should be. See, the Magi hear you saying one thing outwardly, but they do not know that you are thinking another within, and they go on their way so as never to return to you. For he was warning them who, mocking your folly, instructed the Magi to do what the true king had commanded, not what the false one had craftily urged. By another way, says the Evangelist, they returned to their own country (ibid., 12). But when you perceived that you had been tricked by the Magi, Herod, you sought to destroy all the infants of that land, so that you might kill the one you were seeking. But that bridegroom of ours, who came forth from his chamber so as to perfect praise out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, let you fulfil your will, so that an age which could not confess Christ with its own tongue might confess him by the witness of its death, and your monstrous cruelty might be shown, and a throng of infants might be gathered to the marriage of the heavenly bridegroom. Tell me, Herod: if Christ offended you because you heard of his kingship from the Magi's announcements, how did these offend you, the leaders of the Jews who sided with you against Christ, whose sons you killed, afflicting them rather with a most atrocious punishment in their sons? For Christ you could by no means find. But why should I deal with you any longer? I will address the Jews, the Jews themselves, who, while they refused to acknowledge the infant Christ, were compelled to lose their own sons with him: whom indeed Herod, your friend, killed and handed over to death; but on them Christ, whom even now you call your enemy, bestowed immortality and eternal life.

CHAPTER XI. — Against the Jews, from Isaiah and Jeremiah. You, I say, I address, O Jews, who to this very day deny the Son of God. Was that not your voice, when you saw him doing miracles and, testing him, said: How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. But he sent you to consider his miracles, saying: The works that I do, these bear witness of me (John 10:24–25): so that not words but deeds should bear witness to Christ. But you, not acknowledging the Saviour who was working salvation in the midst of your land (Ps. 73:12), adding to evil, said: You bear witness of yourself; your witness is not true. But what he answered you to this you refused to heed. Is it not written, he said, in your Law, that the witness of two men is true (John 8:13, 17)? Transgressors of the Law, attend to the Law. You seek witness concerning Christ: in your Law it is written that the witness of two men is true (Deut. 17:6; 19:15); let there come forth from your Law not only two but even more witnesses of Christ, and let them convict the hearers of the Law, not the doers. Speak, Isaiah, bear witness to Christ. Behold, he says, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us (Isa. 7:14). Let another witness also come forward: you too, Jeremiah, speak, bear witness to Christ. This is our God, he says, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who found out every way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth, and conversed with men (Bar. 3:36–38). See, two fitting witnesses from your Law, by whose testimony your hearts have not been pierced.

CHAPTER XII. — From Daniel. But let more and more witnesses of Christ be brought in from the Law, so that the hardest foreheads of his enemies may be crushed. Let holy Daniel also come, young indeed in age but older in knowledge and gentleness; let him convict all false witnesses: as he convicted the lewd elders (Dan. 13:47), so let him by his testimony crush the enemies of Christ. Speak, holy Daniel, tell what you know of Christ. When the Holy of holies comes, he says, anointing shall cease (Dan. 9:24). Why, in the presence of him whom you insulted, saying, You bear witness of yourself; your witness is not true (John 8:13), did your anointing cease, unless because he is the Holy of holies who had come? If, as you say, the Holy of holies has not yet come but is awaited to come, show the anointing; but if, as is true, your anointing has ceased, acknowledge that the Holy of holies has come. For he is also that stone cut from the mountain without the hands of cutters, that is, Christ born of a virgin without the hands of those embracing; who grew so much that he became a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2:34–35). Of this mountain the prophet says: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord (Isa. 2:3). And of it David says: The mountain of God, a fertile mountain: why do you suspect curdled mountains, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell (Ps. 67:16–17)? For when the Lord Christ himself asked his disciples whom men said that he, the Son of man, was, they answered: Some Elijah, some Jeremiah, some John the Baptist, or one of the Prophets (Matt. 16:14). And he [might say]: Why do you suspect curdled mountains, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell? Peter recognised him, saying: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (ibid., 16). He recognised the mountain, and ascended the mountain: he bore witness to the Truth, and was loved by the Truth. Peter was founded upon the rock, so that he might undergo death out of love for him whom he had three times denied out of fear.

CHAPTER XIII. — The other testimonies from the Law and the Prophets. You too, Moses the lawgiver, leader of the people of Israel, speak, bear witness to Christ. God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers. Every soul that will not hear that prophet shall be cut off from its people (Deut. 18:15, 19). That Christ is called a prophet, hear from Christ himself in the Gospel: A prophet, he says, is not without honour, except in his own country (Matt. 13:57). Let holy David also come forward, a faithful witness, from whose seed came forth he to whom the Law and the Prophets bear witness; let him too speak of Christ. All the kings of the earth, he says, shall worship him; all nations shall serve him (Ps. 71:11). Whom shall they serve? Tell me, whom shall they serve? Do you want to hear whom? The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps. 109:1). And more plainly, and by name: Why, he says, have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2:1–2). Let another witness come forward to him: you too, Habakkuk the prophet, speak, bear witness to Christ. Lord, he says, I have heard your report, and was afraid; I considered your works, O God, and was terrified (Hab. 3:2). What works of God did he marvel at and dread? Did he marvel at and dread the fabric of the world? Far from it: but hear at what he was terrified. In the midst of two animals, he says, you shall be known. Your works, O God: The Word was made flesh (John 1:14). In the midst of two animals you shall be known. What, how far have you descended? You have made me terrified: because you, the Word through whom all things were made, lay in a manger. The ox knew its owner, and the ass its lord's manger (Isa. 1:3). In the midst of two animals you shall be known. What is In the midst of two animals you shall be known, if not either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of the two thieves, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah conversing with him on the mountain? The Word, he says, walked, and went out into the fields (Hab. 3:3). The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. This Jeremiah also says: After this he was seen on earth, and conversed with men (Bar. 3:38). See how the witnesses of truth agree with one another; see how they convict the sons of falsehood. Is this enough for you, O Jews? Or shall we yet, to your confusion, bring in other witnesses from your Law and from your nation, so that they may bear witness to him whom, mocking him with a ruined mind, you told: You bear witness of yourself; your witness is not true? But if I wished to gather from the Law and the Prophets everything that has been said about Christ, time would fail me sooner than material.

CHAPTER XIV. — The testimony of Simeon and Zechariah. Nevertheless I will bring into the midst that old man born of your nation, but not left in your error, holy Simeon, who, though decrepit, was granted to be kept in this light until he should see the true light. Age was indeed already compelling him to go, but he was waiting to receive the one whom he knew was coming. Since this old man had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before he saw the Christ of God, recognising that he had been born, he went to the temple. There, when he saw him carried in his mother's hands, and pious old age recognised the divine infancy, he took the infant in his hands. He indeed was carrying the infant Christ, but Christ was guiding the old man. He who was carried was guiding, so that the other might not be released from the body before the promise. Yet what he said, whom he confessed, mark well, you enemies, not of Christ but of yourselves. Blessing God, that old man cried out and said: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation (Luke 2:26–32). Let also those parents of John, Zechariah and Elizabeth, barren in youth, fruitful in old age, let them too bear witness to Christ. Let them say what they think of Christ, and nourish a fitting witness for Christ. For they say to their newborn little one: You, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways (Luke 1:76). And to the mother herself, the virgin, Elizabeth says: Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting sounded in my ears, the infant in my womb leapt for joy (ibid., 43–44). For John, understanding that the mother of his Lord had come to his own mother, though still placed in the narrow confines of the womb, greeted by movement him whom he could not greet by voice. What [shall I say] afterwards of John himself, forerunner and friend, humble and most faithful servant, made a fitting witness, so much greater among those born of women as he was thought to be what he was not? For the Jews believed him to be the Christ; but he cried out that he was not, saying: I am not the one you suspect me to be; but behold, there comes after me one the strap of whose sandal on his feet I am not worthy to loose (Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; Acts 13:25). O faithful witness, and friend of the true bridegroom, how much would you have humbled yourself if you had said you were worthy to loose the strap of his sandal? But in saying you are not worthy even of this, you contradict the Jews, false witnesses. And these things you said before you saw Christ; and when he himself came to you, exalted yet humble, for the sake of fulfilling his dispensation, to be baptised by you, he who had no sin at all, let the enemies who do not want to hear, hear what you answered, whom you recognised, what witness you brought forth: Behold, he said, the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29, 36). And he added: You come to me to be baptised; I ought to be baptised by you (Matt. 3:14). The servant recognised the Lord; one bound by the chains of original sin recognised him who was free from every bond of sin; the herald recognised the judge, the creature recognised the Creator, the groomsman recognised the bridegroom. For this too is the voice of John: He who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice (John 3:29).

CHAPTER XV. — From the books of the Gentiles. Is this enough for you, O Jews, are such great witnesses enough for you, testimonies from your Law, from your nation? Or will you still dare with shameless mind to say that men of another people or nation ought to bear witness to Christ? But if you say this, he indeed answers you: I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24). But as Paul rebukes you in the Acts of the Apostles: The word of God had to be proclaimed to you first, but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, he says, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46); let us too show that witness was borne to Christ even from the Gentiles, since the truth did not keep silent, crying out even through the tongues of its enemies. When that most eloquent poet said among his songs, Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven (Virgil, Eclogue 4.7), was he not bearing witness to Christ? This might be called into doubt, unless I bring into the midst other fitting witnesses from the Gentiles, who say more. I will not pass over that king who subdued your pride by taking you captive, Nebuchadnezzar, namely the king of Babylon. Tell me, Nebuchadnezzar, you who unjustly cast three just men into the furnace, what you saw in it; tell, tell what was revealed to you. Did we not, he says, cast three men bound into the furnace? And they say to him: Truly, O king. Behold, he says, I see four men loose, walking about in the midst of the fire, and there is no harm in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God (Dan. 3:91–92). O foreigner, whence is this to you? Who announced the Son of God to you? What law, what prophet? He is not yet born into the world, and yet the likeness of the one to be born is recognised by you. Whence is this to you? Who announced this to you, unless the divine fire so enlightened you within that, while the Jews, enemies, were held captive there with you, you should thus bear witness to the Son of God?

CHAPTER XVI. — From the Sibylline prophecies. The prophecy of the Sibyl. But since every word stands on the mouth of two or three witnesses, as the Lord himself, refuting your obstinacy, said: In your Law it is written that the witness of two men is true (Deut. 17:6; John 8:17), let a third witness also be brought in from the Gentiles, so that the witness of truth may be strengthened on every side. Let us bring into the midst what the Sibyl, prophesying, proclaimed about Christ too, so that with one stone the foreheads of both may be struck, namely of the Jews and of the Pagans, and with their own sword, like Goliath (1 Sam. 17:51), all the enemies of Christ may be struck down. Hear what she said: As a sign of judgement, the earth will grow wet with sweat. From heaven the King will come who will reign through the ages, present, that is, in the flesh, to judge the world. Whence the unbelieving and the faithful will see God on high with the saints, at the very end of the age. So souls will be present with flesh, souls whom he himself judges, when the world lies untilled among dense thorns. Men will cast away their idols, and all their treasure too. Fire will burn up the lands, and the sea, and the sky, and, searching, will break open the gates of grim Avernus. But free light will be given to all the flesh of the saints; the guilty the eternal flame will burn. Uncovering hidden deeds, each will then speak his secrets, and God will lay open hearts to the light. Then there will be mourning too; all will gnash their teeth. The sun's radiance is snatched away, and the dance of the stars perishes. The sky will be rolled up, the moon's splendour will fail. He will cast down the hills, and raise the valleys from the depths. There will be nothing lofty or high in human affairs. Now the mountains and the blue waters of the sea are made level with the plains. All things will cease; the earth, shattered, will perish. So springs and rivers alike are scorched with fire. But then the trumpet will send down a mournful sound from on high, lamenting over the world its wretched crime and manifold toils, and the earth, gaping open, will show the chaos of Tartarus. And here before the Lord kings will be set, all together. A river of fire and of sulphur will fall from the heavens.

These things were said about Christ's birth, passion and resurrection, and his second coming, in such a way that if anyone chooses to pick out the first letters of these verses in the Greek, he will find Iēsous Christos Theou Huios Sōtēr: that is, Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour. This also appears when the same verses are translated into Latin, except that the particular character of the Greek letters could not be fully kept.

Listen most attentively to other Sibylline verses, which show Christ's passion more openly: Afterwards he will come into the wicked hands of unbelievers. And they will give God blows with impure hands, and with polluted mouth they will spit out poisonous spittle. But he will simply give his holy back to the lashes. And receiving blows he will keep silent, so that no one may recognise what Word he is, or whence he came, so as to speak to those below. And he will be crowned with a crown of thorns. And for food they gave gall, and for thirst vinegar. They will show this table of inhospitality. For you yourself, foolish one, did not understand your God, playing with the minds of mortals, but you crowned [him] with thorns, and mixed bitter gall. The veil of the temple will be torn, and at midday there will be exceedingly dark night for three hours. And he will die a death, and having taken sleep for three days, then, returning from the dead, he will come to the light. Recalled, he will be the first to show the beginning of resurrection.

CHAPTER XVII. — Testimonies from heaven, from the sea, from the earth, from the underworld. I believe that you, O enemy Jews, are now so overwhelmed and refuted by so many witnesses that you ought to seek nothing further: you who, with excessive folly or rather madness, though you knew everything that had been said and written about Christ, said with shameless face to the Truth himself: You bear witness about yourself; your witness is not true (John 8:13). Nevertheless, so that the truth of the divine majesty may shine out, beyond the illustrious voices of so many witnesses, let all creation proclaim that it has borne witness to its Creator. Did not heaven bear witness, when a new star, at the new birth of a man, as if with tongue and finger, as best it could, pointed out to the nations God born as man? Did not the sea bear witness, when its liquid moisture, in a way forgetting its own nature, took on solidity and bore the imprinted footsteps of its Lord, so that what was said might be fulfilled: Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters (Ps. 76:20)? This element, so as to show how great a difference there is between creature and Creator, would have swallowed in its unstable wave Peter, the servant of Christ who wished to walk upon it, had not the Lord of all things stretched out his hand to the sinking Peter (Matt. 14:31). Did not the earth bear witness, when, mixed with his spittle, he anointed from it the eyes of the man born blind and restored light to one who did not see (John 9:7); and he who had earlier formed the whole man from the earth (Gen. 2:7) repaired by skill from the clay of the earth what his making lacked? Did not the underworld bear witness to Christ, when, having lost its right, it kept Lazarus, whom it had received to be dissolved, whole for four days, so as to return him unharmed when it heard the voice of its Lord commanding (John 11:43)? And what of his passion itself: shall I not, against your shamelessness and savage madness, in a way summon the very light of day as witness? As you supposed, Christ was being killed by you as a man only: and even if that were all he was, you ought to have spared yourselves, so as to keep your hands clear of innocent blood. What blindness was poured into your hearts, that not even that great darkening of the sun at midday deterred you, and the light cut off amid its bright rays? Night was hidden away within the day; rather, night usurped the day, and nature did not keep the course of its order; but the sky is darkened, the earth mourns, the veil of the temple is torn apart, the rocks are split, the underworld is opened (Matt. 27:45, 51, 52); almost all creation is terrified at the death of Christ. And yet amid all these things the eyes of your heart were not opened. O Jews, the demons who possessed your hearts said: We know who you are; why have you come before the time to destroy us (Mark 1:24)? and you [said]: You bear witness about yourself; your witness is not true (John 8:13)!

CHAPTER XVIII. — From the outcome. But, not understanding your own actions, you pleaded our cause. In fact your malice fought for our salvation: for he who had come for this, to die for us, as man did not dread the insane voices of those shouting, Crucify, crucify (Luke 23:21), because as God he had foreseen them beforehand. How hard you laboured to corrupt the disciple Judas with money (Matt. 26:15), and, bad buyers from a bad seller, to purchase Christ whom you were not to possess, conducting a bad market for your souls, when you were paying out the price of our salvation! How hard you laboured to overpower with slanders, setting Caesar's name against him, the judge who was washing his hands of your crime, so that he would accomplish what you wanted done (ibid. 27:24)! How hard you laboured that Christ should be killed and the robber released (ibid., 20–26)! How hard you laboured that Christ should suffer insults, be crowned with thorns (Mark 15:17), be hung on the wood, be pierced with a lance (John 19:34)! How much you shouted, how much you sweated, how much you laboured! But all that labour of yours is our fruit. In fact Christ is killed by you, he rises for us; by you he is hung on the wood and, fastened with nails, is held on the cross, and he is found by our leaders, his disciples, in their midst behind closed doors (ibid. 20:19). By corrupting the soldiers with money you wanted to suppress Christ's resurrection (Matt. 28:12–13), and see, his resurrection is now celebrated throughout the whole world, and what you gave, you have lost entirely. You could not accomplish what you wanted: hear now what you do not want to hear. Rising from the dead on the third day, taken up into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father (Mark 16:19; Luke 24:51); he has scattered you through all lands, so that everywhere you may carry the prophecies of his birth, passion, resurrection, ascension, whatever was said, and may hold out the lamp of the Law to the nations, like wooden lampstands lacking sense. Know that this was done so that the nations should not say that all these things that are done, while they are preached, had been invented by us. That this very dispersion of yours was foretold, the prophet David declares, saying: Do not kill them, lest at any time they forget your law, but scatter them in your power (Ps. 58:12). This dispersion of yours, then, bears witness to Christ, to whom you said, You bear witness about yourself; your witness is not true (John 8:13): so that by your testimony as enemies, other enemies may be confounded, who say that Christ did by magic arts whatever miracles he did. For they also contend that the fact that he is worshipped though dead must be ascribed to magical power. Bring out the prophetic books, O Jews, enemies of Christ, so that from them other enemies, the pagans, may be convicted. Long before he was born he sent the prophets ahead of himself, who foretold all the things we have said above. From this judge now, you who think rightly: if he brought it about by magic arts that he should be worshipped even when dead, was he a magician before he was born? Be confounded, be corrected, you who either think, or believe, or say such things about Christ. Be confounded you too, Jews, who, holding the lamp of the Law in your hands, provide light to others, and do not care to look into it yourselves; but you too indeed wait for him who is to come to come. And he will come; but he will not come as you wish: that exalted one will come who was killed by you though guilty of no crime; he will come manifest as God, and you will see judging the one whom you despised as he worked miracles. What will your conscience be then, when he will no longer show you any patience, because he finds you dead in soul, he who is to come to judge the living and the dead?

CHAPTER XIX. — Against the Arians. We believe in the Holy Spirit, whom we believe to be God, equal to the Father and the Son, abiding in the Father and the Son, inseparable from the Father and the Son, reigning with the Father and the Son. One Trinity, and the third person in the unity is the Holy Spirit, who works all things in all. Him too the Arians blaspheme, wanting him to be less than the Father and the Son. Nor does that fear of the Gospel recall them from their error, which says: If anyone speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but if anyone speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither here nor in the age to come (Matt. 12:32). What is this, Arian? Do you perceive how far your monstrousness has gone? You speak a word against the Son of Man, because you assert that the Son of God is lesser according to his divinity. You speak a word against the Holy Spirit, [saying] that within that very undivided unity he is less even than the Son. By speaking such a word about the Word, and such a word about the Holy Spirit, your sins are not forgiven, neither here nor in the age to come, and do you promise by rebaptising to forgive the sins of others? We acknowledge that the gift of the Holy Spirit is the forgiveness of all sins, with the support of the Truth himself, who after his resurrection said to his disciples: Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven him (John 20:22–23). But you, with sacrilegious daring, in those already baptised, to whom Christ by the gift of the Holy Spirit through Baptism has entirely forgiven all sins, both original and their own, you breathe out Christ in exorcism, you spit out the Holy Spirit; and you strive not to wash the reborn but to defile him; not to free but to bind; not to give life but to put to death. No wonder if you build these ruins daily, you who refused to have Christ, the unbroken rock, as your foundation. The Truth separates his children from your error, and cherishes them so as to nourish them, not as you deceive by flattering so as to kill.

CHAPTER 20. The Resurrection. Know, dearly beloved, that only in the Catholic [Church] is there true faith, genuine peace, everlasting salvation. For it is not in a corner, but is whole everywhere. If anyone departs from it and gives himself over to the error of the heretics, he will be judged as a runaway slave, not as an adopted son: nor will he rise to eternal life, but rather to damnation. For resurrection is promised to the good and the bad alike: We shall all indeed rise, says the Apostle, but we shall not all be changed (1 Cor. 15:51). And what does it profit, my brothers, to rise and not be changed? For whoever has not been changed in this life is found by the just judge to be condemned. And the condemned man does not attain eternal life, he who refused to take the palm of victory over the adversary, the devil. For what does it profit, dearly beloved, that the devil does not hold someone in those chains of the worship of idols, if he possesses him caught and held fast in the birdlime of the heretics? Whoever wishes to reach eternal life must keep strong watch against all the snares of the devil. For that [life] will not be reached in the way this life is.

CHAPTER 21. The difference between temporal and eternal life. Your Charity ought to know how far apart this [life] and that one are. Here falsehood, there truth: here disturbance, there secure possession: here the bitterest bitterness, there everlasting sweetness: here dangerous pride, there carefree exultation: here one fears that he who was a friend may suddenly become an enemy; there a friend always remains a friend, because no enemy is admitted there: here, whatever is good, one fears it may perish; there, whatever you have received will be kept by him who brings it about that you neither perish nor lose what you have received: here death, there life: here mourning, there joy: here all things that God created, there God himself in place of all and in all: and such things as are worthily spoken of, if indeed any are spoken of. For human tongue is not enough to praise what the mind of mortals cannot grasp. We shall come there, my brothers; and there we shall see what the eye here has not seen, there we shall hear what the ear here has not heard, there we shall understand what the human heart here could not grasp (1 Cor. 2:9); seeing and enjoying, we shall exult with unspeakable joy (1 Pet. 1:8). And what joy will there be, where there will be no fear? What joy will there be, when you see yourself a companion of the Angels, a sharer in the kingdom of heaven, reigning with the King, possessing all things while desiring nothing, rich without avarice, administering without money, judging without a successor, reigning without fear of the Barbarians, living without death in eternal life?

CHAPTER 22. On the way to the homeland. But that we may come to these things, let us not abandon the safest way that leads there. What is this way? Christ in his whole self, from the head and from the body. As head, the equal Son, abiding in the Abiding One: as body, lesser, passing swiftly along that way like a giant (Ps. 18:6). Head and body: Christ and the Church. Let us not be separated from him by believing something else about him, as the heretics do; nor from her by turning aside through our depraved morals. This is the true mother, a dutiful mother and chaste, adorned within with the dignity of her husband, not shamefully painted outside with deceiving falsehood. Let no fabricated, alien name lead you away from this mother, let no alien appearance of a church deceive you. She is not the bride of Christ who does not know her husband: she is foul who strives with her words to darken the beauty of so great a husband: in vain does she give herself the name of Church. I see you indeed, O deceitful cave, deceiving because deceived: I see indeed that you fit your form beneath an alien appearance. Why do you make yourself up? Why do you adorn yourself so much? Why do you spread out your fringes? Why do you strive to make yourself equal to the true bride? The bridegroom does not receive you, because you are not the bride. But you say you are beautiful, and you boast of gold and very many ornaments. The bridegroom answers you, he answers you who is fairer in form than the sons of men (Ps. 44:3): You have taken on the look of a harlot, you have become shameless in all things. And if you say, Why? he answers: Because you make yourself up under the appearance of a bride, and you lie that I am your bridegroom. You have taken on the look of a harlot, you have become shameless in all things. You did not call me as Father: For I and the Father are one (John 10:30). You did not call me as Father, and the prince of your virginity (Jer. 3:3–4). These are the words of Christ through the prophet. For if I were the prince of your virginity, I would keep your integrity, as I kept my mother intact. Since, then, you neither acknowledge me as prince of your virginity nor as equal to the Father, neither do I acknowledge you as a virgin. Stop boasting further that you are what you are not: acknowledge your foulness: Arius took away your integrity. You are therefore not a bride, because you are not intact. In vain do you call him bridegroom who is not yours: for Christ does not accept a foul widow. Return, return, you who are repudiated; return, you who are put to shame; return, you who were violated by serpentine frauds; return, not composed in heavenly divinity but entrapped by human assertions, return: you can deceive yourself, you cannot deceive the bridegroom. For he knows the one he seeks, he recognises the one he calls. The mother is always living: stepmother, why do you put yourself in her place? You cannot shut out the beautiful mistress, since you yourself are a foul maidservant. You have taken on the look of a harlot. For you did not keep faith with one husband, you who do not hold to catholic unity. For that bridegroom seeks the true mother, who dutifully nourishes her own children; not the foul one, who fraudulently kills those of another. See what this true mother is, who still bears with you as you smother her children and heap injuries on her husband. She bears with you, because she shows the patience of her bridegroom, and she waits for the breezes of freedom, that her humility may be vindicated by him, since she holds the love of her husband. For it is he who lives and reigns with God the Father and with the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
